Subject: Post-call recap: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling follow-up

Thanks again for taking the time today — great discussion. Below is a concise recap of the performance targets and the autoscaling/burst behaviors we talked through, plus a proposed next steps list so we can lock the POC.

Call highlights / SLO targets you mentioned:
- Latency: p99 <= 300ms for generation requests up to ~256 tokens (p95 target 120ms).
- Throughput: steady-state 120 QPS for bulk generation traffic (spiky burst up to ~450 QPS).
- Concurrency: typical backend concurrency ~200-250 concurrent requests during peak.
- Streaming: token-level streaming required for UI (low-latency token streaming, 50ms chunk flush desirable).

Autoscaling / burst requirements we discussed:
- Warm pools: you'd like a guaranteed warm pool (N GPUs) to absorb sudden bursts with near-instant attach (<10s).
- Cold scale-up: if the warm pool is exhausted, horizontal scaling from cold can be ~45-120s depending on region and image pulls.
- Queueing behavior: acceptable queueing window ~30-60s for non-interactive batch jobs; interactive flows should avoid >5-10s queuing.
- Graceful degradation: acceptable fallback to a smaller model variant for extreme bursts if needed (we discussed ~10-20% quality tradeoff).

Attachments: attaching the SLO_requirements_template.xlsx we use for POCs - please fill in any additional constraints (network, VPC egress, rate of new users, etc.).

Next steps (proposed):
1) Bluefin to confirm the SLO targets + any additional constraints in the template (Evan / Jenna).
2) Redwood to propose a POC plan (2-week perf run) with a warm-pool config and reserved burst policy.
3) Schedule a technical deep dive with your infra team - Vivek to lead and walk through warm-pool ops and queue behavior.
4) Priyom to send trial credits / POC commercial terms and HubSpot link to the deal.

If that all looks good I'll put the tech deep-dive on Thursday (suggest 10:00 PT) and Priyom will follow up on the POC paperwork.

Best,
Marissa
Director, Enterprise Sales | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa - this is helpful and matches our notes. A few clarifying Qs before we fill the template:
1) For the warm pool: can you quantify "guaranteed"? We want a contractable minimum (e.g., 4 GPUs always warm) and to understand the billing impact (are we billed for warm pool instances while idle?).
2) If we exhaust the warm pool and cold scale kicks in, how do you handle backpressure and request ordering? We can tolerate some queuing for batch, but interactive streams need priority.
3) For streaming: is token-level streaming impacted by autoscaling events? We’d like assurances that ongoing streams don’t get interrupted when new capacity is added.

Also tagging Jenna - she’ll own the SLO template input and coordinate with infra.

Cheers,

> Hi Evan - quick answers to your questions and a few implementation notes from an SE perspective.
>
> 1) Warm pool guarantees + billing:
>   - We offer two warm-pool flavors: pre-warmed instances (reserved nodes kept running but not pinned to a customer) and hot-standby (dedicated reserved capacity that you pay for).
>   - If you need a contractable minimum (e.g., 4 GPUs), we recommend Redwood Dedicated reserved hot-standby. That capacity is billed as reserved (monthly commit) but provides sub-5s attach times and deterministic performance.
>   - Pre-warmed shared pools are cheaper (lower idle cost) but are not contractable - they reduce cold-starts statistically and will typically attach <10s but without SLA.
>
> 2) Cold scale-up and backpressure:
>   - Cold horizontal scale-up (new pods/VMs) is ~45-120s depending on region, image layers, and instance startup.
>   - We have a tiered queuing/backpressure model: interactive streams get priority tokens and head-of-line preemption within the queue, while batch requests flow to the standard queue. Queues can be bounded (configurable max queue length) and we expose queue metrics so you can set alarms before SLO breach.
>
> 3) Streaming during autoscale:
>   - Ongoing token streaming uses a session-level connection and KV cache. Adding capacity does not interrupt existing streams - we handle fan-out to additional replicas for new requests; active stream sockets remain attached to the original serving process.
>   - For extreme disruption (if the process is restarted), we support graceful handoff with resume tokens so clients can reconnect and continue without full replay (minor token duplication possible in edge cases).
>
> Recommended config for your workload (based on call):
>   - Reserved hot-standby: 4 GPUs (contracted) to cover immediate bursts.
>   - Pre-warmed shared pool: additional buffer to cover larger multi-minute surges (configurable target % of burst).
>   - Queue policy: interactive priority queue (max 200) with 99th percentile queue latency target <5s; batch queue max 500, target 95th <60s.
>   - Fallback model: smaller model variant for >90s queue to preserve availability (we can quantify quality regression in the POC).
>
> I’m attaching a quick architecture stub that shows warm-pool attach flow and queue tiers (warm_pool_arch.png). Happy to walk through this end-to-end on the deep-dive.
>
> -Vivek
